Angles

The geometry of triangles is a cornerstone of mathematics and physics. In this course, we will be using the properties of similar triangles and right triangles to determine distances and sizes. Specifically, we will be making extensive use of the trigonometric functions sine, cosine, and tangent.

Right triangles

Right triangles are triangles for which one of the three angles is \(90^\circ\). Such a triangle has very nice properties. For example, it has a longest edge, which is the edge not adjacent to the right angle. In the figure above, the right angle is labeled with a corner/hook that looks like \(\Gamma\). Notice that the edge labeled \(C\) is longer than the other two. This edge is called the hypotenuse of the triangle.

Pick one of the two other angles and call it \(\alpha\). In the figure above, we picked it to be the angle opposite the edge labeled \(A\). Because of this, the edge \(A\) is said to be opposite \(\alpha\). Similarly, the edge labeled \(B\) is said to be adjacent.1 Given this naming, it is often useful to relabel the edges as \(H\), \(O\), and \(A\) as in the figure below.

Now let’s look at how the lengths of the edges \(H\), \(O\), and \(A\) depend on each other and on the angle \(\alpha\). Suppose we fix the length of \(A\) and make \(O\) bigger or smaller. Then we can clearly see that both \(\alpha\) and \(H\) get bigger or smaller. We can also switch \(A\) and \(O\) to come to the same conclusion for \(H\), but this time \(\alpha\) will do the opposite. Some experimentation with graph paper and a ruler should convince you that the edges satisfy the following relationship:

\[ H = \sqrt{A^2 + O^2}. \tag{1} \]

This rule is called the Theorem of Pythagoras.

Similarly, the lengths of \(A\) and \(O\) should suffice to determine \(\alpha\): just draw a triangle with some fixed sides \(A\) and \(O\) and then you will see that it gives some angle \(\alpha\) that you can measure with a protractor. If you continue with your experiments, you will also notice that if you double both \(A\) and \(O\), this does not change the angle \(\alpha\). This suggests that there should be a direct relationship between the angle and the ratio \(O/A\). Indeed, there is a special function called the tangent function, abbreviated \(\tan\), that gives this relation:

\[ \tan(\alpha) = \frac{O}{A}. \tag{2} \]

Problem 1

Use geometrical arguments to show that:

  1. \(\tan(0) = 0\)
  2. \(\tan(45^\circ) = 1\)
  3. \(\tan(90^\circ) = \infty\), or undefined if you prefer

Similar considerations imply that there should be special functions to express the angle in terms of the lengths of the hypotenuse and one other edge. They are called the sine, abbreviated \(\sin\), and cosine, abbreviated \(\cos\):

\[ \sin(\alpha) = \frac{O}{H} \qquad \text{and} \qquad \cos(\alpha) = \frac{A}{H}. \tag{3} \]

Problem 2

Use geometrical arguments to show that:

  1. \(\sin(0)=0\)
  2. \(\sin(90^\circ)=1\)
  3. \(\cos(0)=1\)
  4. \(\cos(90^\circ)=0\)

Problem 3

Use the definitions above to show that

\[ \tan(\alpha)=\frac{\sin(\alpha)}{\cos(\alpha)} \]

and check that the special values you demonstrated in Problems 1 and 2 work out.

Notice that it does not matter which angle we picked in the triangle above, as long as you switch what you are calling adjacent and opposite.

Problem 4

Going back and calling the other angle \(\beta\), show that:

  1. \(\sin(\beta)=\cos(\alpha)\)
  2. \(\cos(\beta)=\sin(\alpha)\)

Right triangles are great because they are everywhere.

Problem 5

Below is an image of the Burj Khalifa. Suppose you are admiring this building from your hotel, “The Address Downtown,” the other prominent building in the picture, and you know that the distance to Burj Khalifa is \(B=650\,\mathrm{m}\). You want to know the height of the tallest building in the world, so you pull out the sextant you made in Astro and measure the angle to be \(\alpha=52^\circ\).

  1. Write a formula expressing the appropriate trigonometric function of \(\alpha\) in terms of \(H\) and \(B\).
  2. Solve your formula for \(H\).
  3. Calculate the height \(H\) numerically.
  4. What is the error in height that you are making if your sextant measurement has an uncertainty of \(1^\circ\)?
  5. What is the reported height of the Burj Khalifa?

Problem 7

Below right is a diagram from page 419 of the book. It shows the apparent shift of a foreground star relative to the fixed background stars as viewed from the Earth from opposite sides of our orbit around the Sun. Half the shift angle is indicated in the figure as the “Parallactic angle.” By definition, the foreground star is at a distance of one parsec when the parallactic angle is one second of arc. Note that the radius of the orbit of the Earth is written as \(1\,\mathrm{AU}\). This stands for “astronomical unit” and is by definition the average radius of our orbit.

For Problem 6:

  1. Explain in clear steps how you would use the setup shown in the picture to measure the width of the river.
  2. Suppose you pace out your baseline and conclude it is \(100\,\mathrm{m}\). Suppose you also use your sextant, sideways this time, to measure that the angle at \(B\) is \(60^\circ\). How wide is the river?

For Problem 7:

  1. Convert one arcsecond to degrees.
  2. Use the correct trig relation to express one parsec in AU.
  3. Use \(1\,\mathrm{AU}=1.5\times 10^{11}\,\mathrm{m}\) to calculate how far one parsec is in meters.
  4. It takes light \(500\,\mathrm{s}\) to reach us from the Sun. How long will it take light from the foreground star to reach us?

Radians

A circle of radius \(r\) has a circumference \(C=2\pi r\). If the radius is \(r=1\,\mathrm{m}\), the circle has a circumference of \(2\pi\,\mathrm{m}\approx 6.3\,\mathrm{m}\). Note that we needed to specify a unit of measure of length, but whatever units we choose, \(r=1\) always gives a circumference of \(2\pi\) in the same units.

If we start somewhere on a circle of radius \(r\) and follow the arc of the circle to an angle of \(45^\circ\), how far have we traveled? This arc length \(\ell\) must be an eighth of the circumference, so \(\ell=(\pi/4)r\).

Going around the circle once corresponds to going through an angle of \(360^\circ\). We see that this corresponds to going through an angle of \(2\pi\) in some set of units that is not degrees; we call them radians:

\[ 360^\circ \leftrightarrow 2\pi\,\mathrm{rad}, \qquad 1^\circ \leftrightarrow \frac{\pi}{180}\,\mathrm{rad}\approx 0.0175\,\mathrm{rad}, \qquad 57.296^\circ \leftrightarrow 1\,\mathrm{rad}. \]

Radians have the wonderful property that if an angle \(\alpha\) is given in radians, then the length of an arc with this angle on a circle of radius \(r\) is

\[ \ell = \alpha r \qquad (\alpha\ \text{in radians}). \]

Problem 8

In class you measured the angular size of your outstretched finger by drawing some triangles like in the top figure below. Now, let’s notice that the arc of a large circle is very close in length to a straight line provided the length of the wedge is very large.

  1. Redo your calculation for the angular size of your finger using the triangles and appropriate trig function.
  2. Redo the calculation using the arc length formula to get the angular size in radians.
  3. Convert your answer from part 2 to degrees and compare with your answer to part 1.
  4. The answers you got in parts 1 and 3 should be almost identical. Explain how this can be.

Footnotes

  1. You could complain that the hypotenuse is also adjacent to that angle, but that edge is special. It is the longest. The convention is that the long edge is called the hypotenuse and the shorter one is the adjacent edge.↩︎
